Central Nervous System
Physiology
Properties of Nervous Reflexes

Quick Overview

This lesson covers the general properties of nervous reflexes: unidirectional conduction, localization, total reflex time, irradiation, fatigue, reciprocal innervation, the excitation field with its discharge zone and subliminal fringe, recruitment, occlusion, after discharge, successive spinal induction, and rebound. It also contrasts reflex tetanus with motor tetanus and explains the circuits behind after discharge.

Complete Lesson Content

1. Unidirectional Conduction (Law of Forward Direction)

The nerve impulse runs from the afferent neuron to the efferent neuron and never in the opposite direction. This is due to the synapse, where transmission occurs only from the presynaptic to the postsynaptic neuron.

2. Localization (Specificity)

A specific stimulus applied to a certain receptor produces a specific response in the effector organs of that reflex arc.

Example: a pin prick on the outer surface of the arm produces reflex flexion and adduction of the arm; the same stimulus on the inner surface produces extension and abduction.

3. Total Reflex Time

Reflex time varies from one reflex to another according to the number of synapses. It is very short in the stretch reflex but long in the light reflex.

Components of total reflex time

  1. Conduction time in the afferent nerve.
  2. Central delay (the time taken to cross the CNS).
  3. Conduction time in the efferent nerve.
  4. Latent period of the muscle.

Transmission through one synapse (synaptic delay) takes about 0.5 ms. If the central delay equals one synaptic delay, the reflex is monosynaptic; if it is more, the reflex is polysynaptic.

Central delay (reduced reflex time) = total reflex time − (afferent time + efferent time + latent period of the muscle).

4. Irradiation

The extent of the reflex response depends on the intensity of the stimulus: the stronger the stimulus, the more neurons are activated inside the CNS and the wider the response.

Examples (sole of the foot)

  • Weak, localized painful stimulus: reflex flexion of the big toe only.
  • Stronger stimulus: flexion of ankle, knee, and hip, giving withdrawal of the whole lower limb.
  • Very strong stimulus: withdrawal of the stimulated limb while the other limb extends (the impulse irradiates to it) to support body weight. This is the crossed extensor reflex.

Mechanism: facilitation of interneuronal synapses. Activity in one spinal center irradiates to other centers, causing widespread, complex reactions, for example the mass reflex, which appears a few months after complete transection of the spinal cord.

5. Fatigue

Fatigue is the decline in response caused by repeating the reflex within a short interval.

  • The first site to fatigue is the synapse, due to exhaustion of the chemical transmitter.
  • Fatigue is increased by ischemia, hypoxia, or certain depressant drugs.

6. Reciprocal Innervation

Reflex contraction of one group of muscles is accompanied by reflex relaxation of the antagonistic group, which facilitates movement.

  • Withdrawal reflex: flexors contract while extensors relax. The afferent neuron entering the cord activates two sets of interneurons: one excitatory to the motor neurons of the flexors, the other inhibitory to the motor neurons of the antagonistic extensors.
  • Between CNS centers: for example, inspiratory versus expiratory centers, and cardiac acceleratory versus cardiac inhibitory centers.

Exception: the positive supporting reflex. Pressure on the sole of the foot from body weight makes both extensors and flexors of the limb contract, to support the body.

7. Excitation Field, Subliminal Fringe, and Discharge Zone

The axon of a large sensory neuron entering the spinal cord diverges into many terminals (up to 1000) that end around many motor or other neurons. When the sensory neuron is maximally stimulated, all neurons in contact with its terminals are excited to different degrees; together they form its excitation field.

Neurons inside the excitation field

  • Centrally located (nearby) neurons: receive many collaterals. On maximal stimulation, summation is enough to generate an action potential, so they discharge. This is the discharge zone.
  • Peripherally located neurons: receive few collaterals, so summation is insufficient (only EPSPs develop). They are excited but do not reach firing level and produce no impulse. This is the subliminal fringe.

8. Recruitment (Facilitation)

Recruitment is the overlap of the subliminal fringes of two afferent neurons when both are maximally stimulated at the same time. It increases the number of discharging efferent cells.

9. Occlusion

Occlusion is the overlap of the discharge zones of two afferents when both are maximally stimulated at the same time. It diminishes the number of discharging cells.

Recruitment: subliminal fringes overlap, so more cells discharge. Occlusion: discharge zones overlap, so fewer cells discharge.

10. Recruitment and After Discharge

These properties can be studied by recording the reflex tetanus and the motor tetanus, produced by maximal stimulation of the afferent nerve and of the efferent nerve to the muscle, respectively.

Reflex tetanus versus motor tetanus

FeatureReflex tetanusMotor tetanus
Maximal stimulation ofAfferent nerveEfferent nerve
Latent periodLonger (afferent stimulation plus synaptic central delay)Shorter (short motor end plate delay, resembling a single synaptic delay)
Rise of contractionGradual to a maximum: recruitment, with gradual stimulation of the motor unitsRapid to a maximum: all motor units are excited simultaneously (no recruitment)
After stimulation stopsContraction stays at maximum for a time, then relaxes gradually (after discharge), explained by reverberating circuits of interneuronsMuscle relaxes rapidly; no reverberating circuits and no after discharge
FatigueMay occurDoes not occur (10-fold safety factor of ACh release at the motor end plate)
Power of contractionLimitedHigher (all motor fibers to the muscle are stimulated)

After discharge

  • Definition: persistent discharge from the efferent neuron after a single stimulation of the afferent neuron connected to it.
  • Importance: a physiological phenomenon that explains the mechanism of recent memory.
  • Characters: it may last seconds, minutes, or even hours after the primary stimulus stops, and the presence of interneurons is essential.

Mechanisms of after discharge

  • Open-chain (parallel) circuits (interneuronal barrages): several interneurons are arranged as an open circuit, producing a train of impulses in succession in the output neuron.
  • Closed (reverberating, positive-feedback) circuits: the output neuron is repeatedly activated through a closed circuit of interneurons.

11. Successive Spinal Induction

Augmentation of one reflex by another reflex, which may be synergistic or antagonistic.

  • Positive induction: the reflexes are alike, for example two scratching reflexes, each stimulating the next.
  • Negative induction: two antagonistic reflexes augment each other, for example during walking, where each flexion augments the following extension and each extension augments the next flexion.

12. Rebound

Rebound is exaggeration of a reflex after its temporary inhibition by another, stronger reflex.

Example: a person scratching his head with one hand receives a painful stimulus to that hand. Reflex withdrawal of the limb occurs and the scratching reflex is temporarily inhibited (pain is a prepotent stimulus). After the withdrawal ends, scratching reappears in an exaggerated manner.

Mechanism: accumulation of central excitatory states (a high amount of chemical transmitter) at the synapse during the period of inhibition.

Key Points / Quick Review

Direction and specificity

  • Impulse runs afferent to efferent only, because the synapse transmits from pre- to postsynaptic neuron.
  • A specific stimulus at a certain receptor gives a specific effector response.

Reflex time

  • Depends on the number of synapses: short in stretch reflex, long in light reflex.
  • Synaptic delay is about 0.5 ms; central delay equal to it means monosynaptic, more means polysynaptic.
  • Central delay = total time − (afferent + efferent + muscle latent period).

Irradiation

  • Stronger stimulus gives wider response: big toe, then whole limb, then crossed extensor reflex.
  • Due to facilitation of interneuronal synapses; mass reflex appears months after cord transection.

Fatigue

  • Synapse fatigues first (transmitter exhaustion).
  • Worsened by ischemia, hypoxia, and depressant drugs.

Reciprocal innervation

  • Contraction of one group with relaxation of its antagonists (excitatory plus inhibitory interneurons).
  • Also operates between CNS centers (inspiratory/expiratory, cardiac accelerator/inhibitor).
  • Exception: positive supporting reflex.

Excitation field

  • One sensory axon diverges to up to 1000 terminals.
  • Central neurons form the discharge zone; peripheral neurons (EPSP only) form the subliminal fringe.

Recruitment and occlusion

  • Recruitment: overlap of subliminal fringes, more cells discharge.
  • Occlusion: overlap of discharge zones, fewer cells discharge.

Reflex versus motor tetanus

  • Reflex tetanus: longer latency, gradual rise (recruitment), after discharge, fatigue, limited power.
  • Motor tetanus: shorter latency, rapid rise, no after discharge, no fatigue, higher power.

After discharge

  • Persistent efferent discharge after a single afferent stimulus; explains recent memory.
  • Needs interneurons: open-chain circuits or closed reverberating circuits.

Induction and rebound

  • Positive induction: alike reflexes augment each other; negative: antagonistic reflexes augment each other (walking).
  • Rebound: exaggerated reflex after temporary inhibition, due to transmitter accumulation.
